title: Cycle 14 — Encrypted Session Recovery Package
problem: SessionRecoveryPackageWriter exported the full TriOS session as a plaintext ZIP archive while the manifest advertised local-aes256-gcm-v1 encryption, leaving conversations, browser context, runtime diagnostics, system logs, and companion logs exposed on disk.
root_cause: The writer compressed a plaintext ZIP, computed a SHA-256 manifest over plaintext files, and returned the archive path without ever encrypting. The reader had no decryption path and only understood plaintext ZIPs.
fix: Added TriOSEncryption.recovery named Keychain key. Writer now compresses a staging plaintext ZIP, encrypts it with AES-256-GCM, writes the result as .triosrecovery, and deletes the staging ZIP. Reader decrypts .triosrecovery to a staging ZIP before extraction, and still supports legacy plaintext .zip packages. Package naming and README updated to reflect real encryption. Added SessionRecoveryPackageEncryptionTests.
variants: A: Encrypt the whole ZIP envelope as .triosrecovery — implemented
B: Encrypt each file inside the ZIP — granular but requires custom ZIP logic
C: Replace ZIP with encrypted SQLite/JSON bundle — strongest integrity but breaks tooling
lessons: Manifest claims about encryption must be enforced by the code that produces the artifact, or they become a false security signal.
Whole-archive encryption with a Keychain key keeps the existing ZIP/ditto workflow intact and is the lowest-risk way to harden a diagnostic bundle.
Backward compatibility with legacy plaintext .zip imports costs very little and protects users who have old recovery packages.
